summary: Minos plays as a dice-drafting, engine-building Euro where you draft dice to trigger card-based combo actions, build up tracks, and place warriors for area presence; it feels lush and combo-heavy but suffers from significant downtime and fiddly turns, especially at 3-4 players. Despite a wide array of tracks and bonuses, most of the score actually comes from just two sources (Palace/Decree cards and area majority/presence), making it feel narrower than its length and complexity suggest.
praised: Tense, satisfying dice-drafting mechanic with real push-your-luck/blocking tension
Strong combo-building and engine-building payoff as tracks and cards interact
High production quality and clear player aids from Board&Dice
Solo mode is straightforward to run
criticised: Heavy downtime, especially at 3-4 players (games can run 3.5-5 hours; one reviewer felt 80% of a 4-player game was waiting)
Fiddly, substep-heavy actions that slow the dice-drafting phase down
Scoring is 'point-salady' with lots of minor bonus sources but no real tiebreaker
Despite many mechanisms, only 1-2 sources (Palace/Decree cards, area majority) actually swing the score, making other systems (e.g. boats) feel superfluous
Best experienced at low player counts (1-2), which undercuts its billing as a 1-4 player game

interaction.kind: area majority and open drafting for influence
interaction.detail: Clans place pieces onto one shared map of Crete and compete for area majority/influence in the same regions, so a large part of the board is common contested territory. Players also draft freely from shared card/action options, where taking one can remove it from what an opponent could otherwise take, though there's no direct damage between players.

scoring.how_you_win: Accumulate the most prestige by controlling territories, developing your clan's economy and technology, and completing bonus objectives, with the highest total after the final round crowning the new Minos.

_name: Minos: Dawn of the Bronze Age
